sahne: A cracked wooden shield hangs from his shoulder, and his right arm is bound to his chest from elbow to wrist in a soiled sling. His boots are caked in mire up to the knee and his breath rattles in his chest; in his eyes mingle the bitterness of defeat and a soldier's pride.
sorular: You say you held the stone bridge for two days and nights; why did the castle garrison at the other end of the bridge send no aid, and how was the embankment breached?

The garrison was besieged, master; they had no troopers left to spare for the bridge. The cavalry found a shallow ford along the riverbed with their armored mounts and flanked us from behind. Our shields were splintered, yet we stood till our last breath.
While your sergeant fought on, you took fright and fled without looking back, did you not? A runaway soldier never runs out of excuses!

My sergeant sent me ahead shouting, 'Warn the villages, have them man the battlements!' gatekeeper! Would a coward crawl through mud for two days with a mangled arm? If you doubt me, take this cracked shield and smash it against my chest, but never call me a coward! Fifteen of my comrades fell into the earth at that embankment!
Your anger is just, trooper. Are you ready to report the situation to the warden in the barracks?
I am ready, master! I will spread the map before the warden and point out every culvert the horsemen can cross. Post me on the tower, and if anyone approaches I will sound the horn!
The blood on your arm is fresh and you shiver... Come, let us pour a bucket of water and cleanse your wound.

May God be pleased with you, brother... For three days I feared my arm would rot with gangrene. If I find a pinch of salt and a splash of vinegar, I can bind it myself. A soldier's life is entrusted to the realm.
We have a Roman healer named Miraen in our village; she will tend to your arm.
I have heard of Miraen Hatun's learning, master... Let her cleanse the wound, and by morning I will haul rampart stones even if only with my left hand.
Yesterday we admitted a bowman to the tower; he spoke of the ambush in the pass—did you see him?

The bowman from Tokat? I saw him, master! It was he who rained arrows down upon the brigands from the ridge, shouting that a traitor had shot from behind! If he is safe, our tower is secure; put me beside him and let us stand lookout together.
yarali_gazi
If you are admitted to the barracks, what use will you be with that wounded arm?

In the barracks I will climb the watchtower! Though my right arm is in a sling, with my left hand I can blow the horn and give tactics to the sentries on the wall. I know like the palm of my hand which part of the gorge is craggy and which gives passage to cavalry.
If cavalry approaches, how will you fight with a single arm?
My one arm holds a shield and my chest becomes a rampart, master! I will brace against the gate leaf and trip the horseman's mount. A true soldier never stands idle.
Did anyone else from the sanjak bey's company survive behind you?

Our sergeant was still swinging his sword by the ditch when last I saw him... He sent me ahead saying, 'Run to the ridge and carry word to the villages behind.' I fulfilled my duty and reached your gate.

yanitlar.kabul: Bless you, master guard. I will find clean water by the infirmary wall and wash my wound, apply Miraen Hatun's salve, and take my turn on watch when called.
yanitlar.ret: Will you drive me beyond the trench with this bleeding arm? By night the cavalry patrol sweeps the plain; you will find my lifeless body in the brush... May the sin be upon your neck.
yanitlar.kisla: Bring me straight before the castle warden! The embankment in the gorge has collapsed, and I must show the horsemen's route upon the map. Let one more life be pledged to the barracks.

not: Accept, Reject, and Barracks from the start.
acilis: My shield is cracked and my arm is in a sling, master guard... We held the stone bridge behind us for two days and two nights, yet the cavalry broke through the embankment. Even if I have no strength left for pitched battle, I have eyes to keep watch at your gate and breath to warn of approaching peril.

sahne: Forged copper bowls and ladles clatter against one another inside his donkey's saddlebags. His apron is smeared with hearth soot, and the gash above his left brow has not yet scabbed over; suspicious metallic weights can be felt at the bottom of his pack.
sorular: You say you fled along the creek when the marketplace was raided; with the copper bowls clattering in your saddlebags all down the valley, how did brigands not pursue you?

I stuffed dry grass and felt between the bowls, master! I even wrapped felt around the donkey's hooves so not a sound would escape. By night I mingled with the rushing sound of the creek and slipped past the crags. A craftsman knows how to be resourceful.
Why is the bottom of that large cauldron on your donkey's back double-riveted? Is there smuggled metal inside?

Hush, master, I beg you... Inside the double bottom I hid not smuggled ore, but pure mercury powder sought by alchemists and an ingot of refined tin! While the bazaar was being looted, I concealed them so they would not fall into brigand hands! If it comes to light, Master Karaca will drive me from his hearth! I will give you whatever you ask, only do not announce it to the folk!
If you donate that metal to Master Karaca's smithy, the gate will open.
Agreed, master, upon my head! Let Master Karaca use it for the smithy and apply mercury solder to the village shields! Only let me practice my craft in this village!
The cut on your brow is fresh and your eyes are full of dust... Do you have a morsel of food?

I had two pieces of dry biscuit in the donkey's feedbag, and I shared those with the beast, master. If you give me a bowl of hot soup, I will polish all the sooty pots in the village till they gleam like gold.
The village cauldrons await tinning before winter so they do not taint the food with verdigris.
I will light the hearth early tomorrow morning, master! Sal-ammoniac smoke will curl through the square, and all the copperware will shine like a mirror.
We admitted the cobbler journeyman who came yesterday; he has already begun stitching shoes.
That orphan apprentice from the bazaar? Ah, his stitching is sound, master! Let him sew the shoes and I will polish their brass buckles; let the village market come alive again!
supheli_bakirci
There is little copperware in our village; the folk use clay pots. What use is a tinsmith here?

Clay cracks and shatters, while copper lives a thousand years, gatekeeper! You must tin the village soup cauldron so it does not poison the broth. I also forge horseshoes and door hinges; my hand knows every metal.
What is that gash on your brow—were you in a brawl?
As I fled, the great cauldron atop the workbench toppled over, master. Trying to catch it, its rim split my brow. A copper edge cuts skin, yet love of the craft stands above life.
Are the bowls in your saddlebag lawful goods, or did you gather them from the looting?

I am a tinsmith registered in the Ahi line, master! Stamped on the bottom of every bowl is my own hammer mark. Not a single scale of metal I did not forge by the sweat of my brow has ever entered my bag.

yanitlar.rusvet: Look here, master... Let me leave you this fine cast yellow copper bowl so you may drink soup by the hearth, and let the mercury solder powder beside it be my gift as well. Do not let Master Karaca hear of it—keep it between us and draw back the bolt.
yanitlar.kabul: I will tie the donkey in a sheltered corner of the courtyard and toss two handfuls of hay before the beast, then curl up beneath the awning myself. First thing tomorrow I will polish the village cauldrons and pay my respects to Master Karaca.
yanitlar.ret: I cannot stay out in the open country alone with this load, gatekeeper! Looters who hear the clatter of copper will fall upon my throat. Was this the whole of your mercy?

not: Bribe, Accept, and Reject from the start.
acilis: I am a tinsmith of the lower districts, gatekeeper... My donkey carries the bowls, and I lead the donkey's halter. When the marketplace was raided, amidst naphtha and smoke I loaded my saddlebags and climbed up along the creek bed. Grant me a hearth corner so the cauldrons of this village do not go untinned.

sahne: In his arms he holds a frail goat kid whose broken left leg is splinted with wood. His felt vest is torn to shreds and his bare knees bleed from thorn scratches; he presses the kid to his chest like an infant.
sorular: You say you could not leave this lame kid when brigands raided the fold; while the flock scattered up the mountain, who was the chief of those brigands, and why did they not shoot you along the creek?

It was the band of the Red-Bearded brigand, master! They chased after the fattened rams in the fold and did not even glance at this poor lame kid. Taking the little one in my arms, I turned onto the goat path at the foot of the cliff.
It was not wolves that raided the fold, but the Red Crow brigands to whom you owed debt, was it not? You will draw their trail to this village!

Yes, I had a debt, master... Last winter when the fold collapsed I borrowed three coins from a usurer, and the brigands demanded ten sheep in interest! When I could not pay, they torched the fold! I scattered the flock onto the mountain so the debt could not be seized! What fault has this kid? The fault is mine—punish me as you will, only do not cast this innocent creature to the wolves!
If brigands are on your trail, we must put the village sentries on alert.
Alert them, master! I waded through the water along the creek bed so even their hounds cannot find my scent. Yet if brigands come, I will haul firewood to the barracks and hold a spear too!
Your knees bleed from bramble thorns and your felt vest is in tatters... The little one in your arms is shivering.

I rubbed thyme oil on the kid's leg and bound it with wood splints, master. If we find a palmful of warm milk and a wisp of dry straw, within two weeks it will stand on its feet and be a companion to Yusuf's goat Karabash.
Yusuf also lost his goat on the mountain like you; you will be glad to meet him.
I heard of Yusuf's name on the mountain... His mother's prayer watches over him. I will entrust this kid to Yusuf; let the two of them run across the village meadow.
Yesterday we admitted the highland shepherd with his ewes Akcha and Karaca into the fold; do you know him?
Highlander Dursun? Ah, master, his ewe Akcha has abundant milk! Let him milk the ewes and give two sips to this orphaned kid, and the kid will be on its feet within two days!
topal_oglak
The village fold is full; why should we make room for a stranger shepherd?

Though I am a stranger, I know the wolves and birds of the mountain, master. I know which herb holds healing and which spring is poisoned. I will tend your flock like my own child and let no harm come to a single hair.
What is that wooden splint tied to its leg—will the bone knit?
Its leg split while leaping down the crags. I tied two dry branches and rubbed thyme oil over it. In two weeks it will stand up and skip like a true goat, bringing blessing to this village's fold.
If the brigands follow the creek trail, will the village not be endangered?
I walked against the current of the water, master; my tracks vanished in the floodwater. Have no fear—I will cast no shadow upon the fortress of this village.

yanitlar.ret: I will curl up at the base of the stone and pull my torn felt vest over the kid. Without blinking an eye I will wait for dawn, though the frost is bitter... If its life gives out, may the sin rest upon your neck.
yanitlar.kabul: May God never bring sorrow to your hearth! I will sleep in a corner of the fold; let this mute creature grow up beside Yusuf, and let me take root in the soil of this village. I will be a burden to no one.

not: Reject and Accept from the start.
acilis: I am the shepherd of the fold on the slope... Last night when brigands raided the fold, I turned the flock loose onto the mountain, yet I could not leave this lame kid behind. Carrying this little one in my arms, I crossed the crags. Just show us an eave and a handful of dry straw.

sahne: A heavy salt sack sewn of coarse linen swings from his hemp belt. His hands are cracked from frost and salt burn, and dried salty sweat gleams on his left temple; a faint smell of sulfur rises from the bottom of the sack.
sorular: You say the salt lake caravan was ambushed on the steppe; while the mules were driven over the cliff, where were the khan guards along that route, and how did you hide the salt at your sash?

The khan had been left far behind, master; they laid an ambush in the middle of the steppe and stampeded the mules over the ravine. I crouched in a rock crevice and buried this salt bag against my chest. Salt is life; a man left without salt on the mountain rots away.
Salt is white; what is this ash-colored, sulfur-smelling powder at the bottom of your sack? Do you carry gunpowder saltpeter?

Master... A merchant weighs every mineral. On the rocky slope of the salt lake we found a vein of saltpeter... The caravan master said we could sell it to castle wardens for good coin. I harbor no ill intent! Take this saltpeter and give it to the village barracks so they may pour fuses at the foot of the wall! The bread earned from salt is enough for me!
If you surrender the saltpeter to the barracks, no reckoning will be demanded of your caravan.

I surrender it gladly, master! Let the saltpeter go to the barracks, and let the pure rock salt enter your granary! This winter the villagers' meat will not spoil and their cheese will stay firm as stone.
Your hands are cracked from salt burn and the fissures are filled with blood... You must be in pain.

Salt burns a wound, yet it also kills the rot, master. My weariness comes from the weight of the salt. Give me a bowl of hot water to wash my cuts, and I will donate half the salt to the village granary.
Salt was nearly exhausted in our village granary; you arrived just in time.
Khidr sent me, master! All winter long I will cure the provisions of the granary so not a single piece of meat goes to waste.
Yesterday we admitted a tinsmith whose saddlebag held yellow copper bowls.

Master Mahmut the coppersmith? I know him, master—we drank soup together at the Kayseri khan! If he polishes the copper bowls, I will fill them with pure rock salt, and the village table shall be enriched!
tuz_kervani_kacak
Salt is scarce in our village granary; will you let us have it cheaply?

I am no profiteering merchant, master. Grant me a hayloft to shelter my head and a bowl of hot bulgur at dusk, and I will donate half the salt to your granary. With the rest I will barter fairly in the village.
Is the salt at your sash pure white, or muddy sediment from the lake?
It is pure mountain salt, crystal-white rock salt, master! It has never touched mud. A single pinch keeps a whole cauldron of meat from spoiling and holds cheese firm as stone.
Have the looters on the steppe turned this way?
They were busy plundering the silk bales and silver in the caravan, scattering the salt on the ground as dead weight. It will take them two days to reach here—make your preparations.

yanitlar.kabul: May you find abundance, gatekeeper! By the edge of the hayloft I will set the salt upon a dry plank and lie down beside it. All winter long I will not leave the meat and cheese of this village unsalted.
yanitlar.rusvet: Master guard... Let two handfuls of crystal salt and a pinch of saltpeter powder be poured into your pouch. In a frontier beylik it is more precious than silver. Add it to your soup and see your winter through; just let me inside.
yanitlar.ret: If I stand out in the open on this mountain peak, by night the jackals will catch my scent and come for the salt. I will hide behind the rocks and wait till dawn, yet if I lose my salt I am ruined.

not: Accept, Bribe, and Reject from the start.
acilis: I am a peddler who outfits caravans from the salt lake to carry goods to mountain villages, gatekeeper... Our caravan was ambushed on the steppe road and the mules were driven over a cliff. I could salvage only this fine rock salt at my sash. There is neither food nor realm without salt; open the gate so your village may prepare for winter.

sahne: A bent copper bugle hangs from the thick leather strap around his neck. His leather vest is split at the shoulder and the wooden scabbard of the sword at his waist is cracked; a fresh graze on his temple trickles blood down his cheek, and in his eyes lingers an averted look of kinship shame.
sorular: You say you lit the beacon before the tower was torched; how many times did you sound the horn before the tower fell, and did the sentry sergeant on the plain not catch your signal?

I blew three bitter blasts, master! The sound of the horn echoed across the valley. Yet they had raided the outpost on the plain at the same hour; when I saw the smoke, I knew it had fallen too. Had I not leaped from the cliff, I would have burned alive.
They say someone of your own blood was among those who raided the tower, and that is why you cut the horn blast short; is it true?

Who... Who told you that? Master... My uncle's son rode at the head of the brigand troop! 'Blow that horn and I will cut your breath!' he shouted! For a moment... For just a single moment I froze! Yet then I touched fire to the beacon and hurled myself over the cliff! I did not betray my post, master—blood ties clouded my mind for an instant, yet it was still I who came to warn your gate!
Even if he is your kinsman, if he approaches the border of this village he will be met with spears!
I know, master... Since he turned brigand, I have no kinsman left! I will blow my horn atop this village's tower so fiercely that even my cousin will tremble at my voice!
Your leather vest tore when you leaped from the cliff, and blood trickles from your temple... Catch your breath.

I tumbled down the cliff into the brush, master. Scratches matter little; the copper of my bugle is dented, yet its breath is sound. Give me a sip of water and let me climb the tower to stand lookout.
Our tower's bugle was broken; your arrival is a blessing.
Post me at the very top of the tower! I will spot cavalry dust from two miles off and rouse the village with a voice like the call to prayer.
Yesterday we admitted the wounded trooper into the infirmary; he told us the bridge embankment had collapsed.

The trooper from the stone bridge? Praise be that I see him alive! If he brought word of the embankment, I bring intelligence of fifty mounted raiders on the ridge; let the warden hear us both and take precautions!
borazanci_korkaklik_ithami
Your bugle was bent when you leaped from the cliff; does this copper still give voice?
Copper bends, yet its voice never bends, gatekeeper! The blast of this bugle will rouse the village from two miles away. Post me atop the rampart and let my eye watch the plain.
How many men raided the tower, and what color was their banner?
There were at least fifty horsemen, master! Wearing black fur caps, with wolf tails tied to the tips of their lances. They split into three columns and are sweeping down the valley.
Why should we not clap you in irons for taking fright and abandoning your post?

With the tower blazing like tinder, had I stayed inside I would have turned to ash, master! What use is a charred soldier to anyone? I saved my life to bring warning; even if you chain me, that is the truth.

yanitlar.kisla: Take me straight to the warden! I will describe step by step the dry creek bed the horsemen from the plain will follow, and hand my bugle to the lookouts on the tower so we do not lose this village to a raid.
yanitlar.ret: Will you leave me as an open target on this plain? Within two hours the horsemen will descend into the valley; you will find my corpse before your gate... May the sin rest upon your neck.
yanitlar.kabul: Bless you, brother. I will crouch at the foot of the infirmary wall and catch my breath, wipe the blood from my temple, gird my sword, and stand watch at the gate tonight.

not: Barracks, Reject, and Accept from the start.
acilis: I am the bugler of the hilltop watchtower, gatekeeper! The tower was raided; I lit the beacon torch, yet they rained arrows from the cliff. When the lower floor was set ablaze, I leaped from the precipice and tumbled into the valley. The dust of the horsemen behind me has not yet settled—open the gate so I may warn the warden!

sahne: In his arms he cradles a dry grapevine sapling whose roots are wrapped in damp burlap. The handle of the pruning knife at his sash is darkened with sweat; his palms are blistered and cracked, and the scent of fresh earth and sour grape must rises from the cloth around the sapling.
sorular: The village needs bread, vintner; where shall we find the patience to wait three years for grapes?

Does a grapevine yield grapes alone, master? From its leaves stuffed rolls are wrapped, from its unripe clusters sour verjuice is pressed, and from its raisins strength is found all winter long! A people who plant no vines perish in a single winter; a man who thinks of tomorrow plants a vineyard.
A sharp smell of sour must rises from the cloth wrapped around the graft shoot at your breast! Is this a Frankish wine-vine cutting forbidden by the zealots?

Master... A vineyard has both its lawful and its forbidden uses! This vine is a honey-muscat grape smuggled across the Byzantine border! A zealot may mistake it for wine, yet its dried raisins give strength to soldiers all winter and healing to the sick! If the village preacher objects, I will give its leaves to the soup kitchen and boil its molasses for the children! Do not snap the root, master!
If you share your knowledge with our village healer Miraen Hatun, permission will be granted to plant the vineyard.
Miraen Hatun knows the salve of the vine root as well, master! I will give her cuttings for medicine and grape leaves to Sister Ayse! Only let the sapling touch the soil!
Your palms are cracked, and you warmed the root against your chest so it would not dry out... A sip of our water is lawfully yours.

May God be pleased with you, master... I stinted my own throat to sprinkle water upon the root. If the root dies the vineyard dies, and if the vineyard dies hope dies. Give me the southern slope, and within two years the arbors will be painted green.
Our southern slope is stony, yet it catches plenty of sun; it will suit the vine.
The grapes of stony soil grow sweet, master! Gravel keeps the root warm and enriches its sugar. I will turn that slope into a paradise.
Yesterday we admitted a young peasant carrying grape must in his jug; are you kin to him?

The lad with the clay jug? I know him, master—he is an orphan from our upper valley! It was I who filled his jug with the last must of the camp! If that lad is safe, this sapling will not remain an orphan; we will pour his must upon the root of this sapling and awaken its abundance!
You say you were the vineyard watchman of the lower valley, whose grapes went to the beylik cellar; what did those who burned the vineyard do to the villagers, and why did they leave you alive?

They drove the villagers down to the valley floor, master, and torched the vineyard cottages. I hid inside the culvert of the aqueduct, and they took me for dead. When the fire died down to embers, I cut this lifeblood graft shoot from the soil and fled.
Did this sapling wrapped in cloth not freeze on the road?
At every spring I dampened its cloth and warmed it with the vapor of my own chest, master. The scent of ancestral soil still lingers on its root; the day you plant it, it will put forth shoots.
saraplik_bag_suphesi
Besides pruning vines, what use will you be to the village in winter?
In winter I weave baskets from pruned shoots, mend fences, and graft fruit trees. If a farmer's hand stops, his blessing flees; my hand never stops.

yanitlar.ret: I will crouch against the outer wall of the caravanserai and bury the sapling in damp mud. I can pass the night at the base of the stone, yet if the sapling withers my heart will burn...
yanitlar.kabul: May your soil rejoice, master guard! I will plant this sapling on the southern slope. Within three years the children of this village will come to your gate with armfuls of grapes, and I will offer its healing to Miraen Hatun.
yanitlar.rusvet: Look here, master... One is a honey-fig shoot and the other a seedless grapevine cutting. Plant them in your own garden and in two years you will harvest their fruit. Let these be yours, and bid me enter.

not: Reject, Accept, and Bribe from the start.
acilis: I am the vineyard watchman of the lower valley, gatekeeper... They set the vines ablaze, yet I dug up this fine graft shoot from the soil and tucked it into my breast. To one who waits three years in patience, this vine yields honey-sweet grapes. Grant me a slope and a span of earth so I may plant your vineyard.

sahne: An itinerant weigher whose brass dirhem weights clink at his sash and who carries a small hand balance in a leather pouch at his breast. The hem of his kaftan is torn and blood oozing from his heel is caked with mud; fine file marks glint upon the brass weights.
sorular: You say the market at the waystation khan was scattered; where is the caravan master of the khan, and did you not see the innkeeper or the sentries as you tucked your balance into your sash?

The innkeeper locked the doors, yet they smashed the gate with axes, master! To save the goods, the caravan master leaped onto his horse and rode into the woods. I wrapped my dirhem weights and balance into my sash and escaped up the kitchen chimney.
Hand me those dirhem weights! Why is the bottom of this five-dirhem brass block filed down? Did you do this to rob the villagers?

Master... When weighing at the judge's court a burr remained on the brass, so I filed it smooth! Not for fraud... That is, the merchants used coarse weights, and I wanted to protect my share! Very well... I confess: that five-dirhem piece is a quarter-grain short! When I could not pay the market extortion tax, I was forced to use that weight! Smash that weight, master! Take my scale if you must, only let me into the village so I may weigh with justice!
We have smashed the shaved weight! With the remaining sound weights you shall weigh the village market honestly!
Smash it, master, gladly! Let the crooked weight melt away and lift the sin from my neck! With my true weights I will not let a single grain of wheat in the village be weighed short!
hileli_dirhem
Your heel is torn open and blood is caked with mud... You can barely walk.

While running up the rocky footpath my leather sock split and a sharp stone pierced my heel bone, master. It burns with pain, yet the honor of a craft is greater than an aching foot. Two days of rest in a hayloft will suffice for me.
We have a salt merchant in our village; we will have salt water pressed to your wound.
A salt merchant? His rock salt will draw out the inflammation in my heel, master! It will sear the wound clean, and by morning I will take my place at the village scales.
Yesterday we admitted the rock-salt merchant; had you weighed his salt bales?

Ilyas the salt trader? Yes, master! Before the caravan was raided, he weighed his salt sacks upon my very balance! Let him bring the salt and I will set the dirhem weight, so the villagers may barter penny for penny!
How will you stand in the marketplace with that crippled foot?

My leather sock tore while running up the stony trail and my heel split open. If I rest two days in a corner of the hayloft, it will scab over. Even if the foot stays lame, the hand that holds the balance never trembles.
Are your remaining brass dirhems full weight, and do they bear the judge's stamp?
The other weights bear the sealed stamp of the sanjak judge, master! We cast the shaved one away; with the remaining weights, whatever is rightful comes out true.
Did the looters follow behind you?
They were slashing open the bales and scattering the wool, so they took no notice of me. I struck out up the goat path behind the stable toward the ridge. No one is following me.

yanitlar.rusvet: Brother guard... Here is a solid cast brass dirhem weight. Melt it down in the market and it fetches a tidy sum of coin. Hook it to your belt and let it be your due—only unbar the gate.
yanitlar.ret: With this mangled heel I cannot take a step across the open plain, gatekeeper... I will lean against the awning post and wait, yet if the breath of wolf and jackal touches the back of my neck tonight, I will not forgive my right.
yanitlar.kabul: May the scales of justice never waver! I will hold the balance in the village market and let no man cheat another of his due. A just market brings blessing to a village.

not: Bribe, Reject, and Accept from the start.
acilis: I am a weigher who travels the highlands weighing wool and dyer's madder, gatekeeper... When the market at the waystation khan was broken up, I tucked my balance into my sash and bolted up the mountain. The scale weighs true, and when the hand holding it is honest, the market finds abundance. If you have a market, you have need of me.

sahne: On his back he carries a coarse mortar shovel with an iron blade. His fingertips are cracked and scabbed from lime burn; a fresh bruise from a falling stone stands out on his right shoulder, and his voice rumbles loud and fierce like a trench wind.
sorular: You say you grabbed your shovel and escaped through the culvert when the worksite was raided; is that huge bruise on your shoulder from a falling stone as you fled, or from the castle warden's cudgel?

As I fled, a cornerstone broke loose from the rampart face, master. I had laid that stone with my own hands; it turned out they had stinted the mortar, so the stone slipped and crushed my shoulder. Yet the warden's cudgel was no light matter either—we took plenty of threats because we saw those who stole from the mortar.
A wall does not collapse by itself! You saw the castle warden stealing lime and dressed stone from the mortar, and they beat you to silence you, did they not?

How did you know, gatekeeper? Yes! The warden had the lime hauled to his own vineyard and stuffed rotten rubble into the base of the rampart! Because I said, 'This wall will cave in at the first trebuchet stone,' they brought a timber beam down across my back and threw me into the moat! I crawled out through the water culvert of that moat! This village's palisade is made of wood too; he who knows not mortar is left without a fortress in two days!
A laborer who speaks the truth is welcome among us. Can you lay a stone foundation beneath our village's wooden palisade?

Stone foundations are my trade, master! I will pour such lime mortar around the base of the stakes that even if a Mongol battering ram strikes, the timber will not budge! Just provide me stone and lime!
rusvetci_dizdar_tanigi
Your fingertips are cracked from lime burn and dripping blood... Does it not hurt?

If a laborer's hand does not touch lime, it never grows calloused, master! It burns, yet I feel it no longer. Give me a bucket of water to wash off the lime; I am content with dry bread and a trench to shelter my head.
We have lime pits in our village; you can take up your work.
I will clean out the lime pits with my own hands! I will slake the quicklime with water and boil it so the rampart mortar sets hard as rock.
Yesterday we admitted a bowman to the tower; he complained of the weakness of the parapets.

The bowman on the tower spoke true, master! The base beneath the crenel is hollow; if two horsemen pull at it, the parapet will give way. Let him shoot the arrows, and I will lay stone beneath the parapet! Together we two will hold the wall like steel.
Our village wall is built of wooden stakes; what work is there for a stonemason here?

Wooden stakes are at the mercy of fire, gatekeeper! Who will lay the stone footing and lime fill around the base of the stakes? If you do not build the gate threshold of stone, cavalry horses will smash right through. Give me a shovel, and I will ring the village with trenches.
Can you swing a shovel with hands burned raw by lime?

If a laborer's hand never sees lime, it never forms calluses, master! It stings, yet I pay it no mind. I will knead mud with mortar and fortify the weakest stretch of the moat like a fortress in two days.
Will you join the barracks and dig trenches?
Digging the barracks moat is my bounden duty. A trench-digger knows well which soil caves in and where to dig a wolf-pit. It is the breastwork that saves a soldier's life.

yanitlar.kabul: Bless you, gatekeeper. I will sit on a stone and hold my shovel across my knees. Let me find a bowl of water to wash off the lime, and at first light I will be at the foot of the wall.
yanitlar.kisla: Send me straight to the barracks! I will show you which side of the trench is loose, reset the collapsed stones, and dig breastworks for the guards.
yanitlar.ret: I will climb down into the dry bottom of the ditch before the gate and lean on my shovel. If a wolf comes by night I will meet it with the iron blade, yet if this village's rampart collapses you will remember me.

not: Accept, Barracks, and Reject from the start.
acilis: I am a laborer who hauls stone and mixes mortar in the castle moat, gatekeeper... The worksite was raided; when horsemen lined the edge of the ditch, I grabbed my shovel and ran up through the culvert. My hands are split from lime, yet my body is hard as stone; I have come to build up your rampart and granary.

sahne: A hornbeam rolling pin hangs from his neck by a cord, and on his back he carries a dough trough carved from thick ash wood. His flour-dusted tunic clings to his chest with sweat, and a deep friction scrape marks his elbow; the sweet, tangy scent of sourdough starter wafts from his trough.
sorular: You say when horsemen burst into the bakery you leaped out the flour chute with your dough trough; how did you fit a huge trough through that narrow chimney, and what became of the flour sacks behind you?

It is a hornbeam trough left by my father, master—narrow in width and long in body. We had built the chute wide so flour dust would not clog it. The looters ripped open the sacks and the flour mingled with smoke; I pulled the trough through and jumped from the roof into the hayloft.
The flour residue at the bottom of your trough has turned black; is that poisonous ergot of rye? Do not poison the villagers!

I beg you do not say so, master! That is no poisoned rye—it is buckwheat sourdough starter roasted with black cumin! It is the forty-year-old sour starter of our hearth! Mix this starter into a bushel of flour, and by morning the rising dough will fill the whole village square with the fragrance of bread! Whoever eats of it on an empty stomach will feel his lungs rejoice!
The scent of bread is the morale of the villagers. Can you relight the village bakery oven?
I will light it, master! From the river stones of the village I will build a glowing tandoor, and for the soldiers I will bake campaign hardtack that keeps for three months without spoiling!
zehirli_un_suphesi
Your elbow is scraped raw and your floury tunic clings to your back with sweat... You are worn out.

I scraped it against the wall while jumping from the roof into the hay, master; so long as a baker's soul stays with his dough trough, he feels no pain. Give me a bowl of hot broth, and by morning I will pull the first loaf from the oven and bring it to your gate.
In our village the flour granary is under the stewardship of Saruca Hatun.
I know the blessing of Saruca Hatun! I will take her flour into my trough and spread abundance through the village without wasting a single flake of bran.
Yesterday we admitted a farmer with a broken plow who had saved his barley seed.

Uncle Idris the barley-grower? Ah, master, let us grind his barley at the mill, and from the barley flour I will bake winter loaves for the villagers! Together we two will never let the village go hungry!
The village flour is scarce and winter is near. Will a baker not drain the granary dry?

A master baker does not waste flour—he draws abundance out of flour, gatekeeper! Without sifting away the bran I knead whole wheat, and I bake soldiers' hardtack so well that it does not go stale for three months. From a single handful of flour I feed ten souls.
Did you get that bloody scrape on your elbow while falling down the chute?
I grazed the wall while leaping from the roof into the stable hayloft, master. The bone is sound. So long as a baker's hand kneads dough, an aching elbow is forgotten once two loaves are baked.
Do you have bricks to build an oven?
I will build a tandoor from the river stones of the village and plaster it with clay. Within two days the tandoor will glow red-hot, and the village folk will see the face of warm bread.

yanitlar.ret: I will hold the trough over my head as a shield and curl up beneath the awning. The frost will scatter my flour, yet I will guard my life. When the gate opens in the morning, I will seek my fortune again...
yanitlar.rusvet: Master... I have two pieces of fine dry biscuit baked with fragrant black cumin that I saved from the oven. Crumble them into your soup for flavor. Put them in your pouch and draw back the bolt.
yanitlar.kabul: May your hearth never know sorrow! By the edge of the hayloft I will set the trough beneath me and rest. Tomorrow morning give me the first flour from Saruca Hatun's granary, and I will set the tandoor smoking.

not: Reject, Bribe, and Accept from the start.
acilis: I am the baker of the waystation khan, gatekeeper... When horsemen burst into the bakery and looted the pantry, I shouldered my dough trough and leaped out through the flour chute. My trough is on my back, my rolling pin around my neck... Give me a bushel of flour, and by morning I will fill the village square with the warm scent of fresh bread.

sahne: Long farrier's pincers and a pair of iron horseshoes hang from his leather belt. His tunic is soaked in forge soot and sweat; his left heel is bound with a torn, soiled cloth stained with mud and clotted blood, and a notched brand upon the horseshoes gleams ominously.
sorular: You say the stallion snapped its chain and a horseshoe nail pierced your heel; how did a man with a nail in his foot crawl through that moat culvert, and why did the brigands not shoot you?

I clenched my teeth and yanked the nail out with my pincers, master! Then pressed mud and horse dung over it to staunch the blood. The brigands chased after the stallion, and no one looked twice at a limping farrier's apprentice. Crawling over the crags, I reached your gate.
That pair of horseshoes at your belt bears the three-notched brand of the Red Crow brigands! Are you the smith who shoes the outlaws' horses?

Master... They pressed a sword to my throat! In the Karaboran pass they cut off the caravan and told me, 'Either trim and shoe our horses' hooves or we throw you down the well!' Yes, I shod them... In fear for my life I shod them! Yet into the hoof of the last stallion I purposely drove the nail crooked so the mount would stumble! When that stallion reared up, the nail flew into my own heel! I am no traitor, master—I lamed the outlaw chief's horse and escaped!
If you lamed the outlaw's mount, the warden of the barracks will want to hear you.
Take me to the warden, master! I will show upon the map how many of the brigands' horses are limping and which footpath they will take! The horseshoes at my belt are the proof!
harami_ati_nali
The mud and dried blood on your heel reek of gangrene... You must go to the infirmary at once.

My life is at my lips, master... I can no longer tread upon it. Have the wound cleansed and steeped in salt water at Miraen Hatun's infirmary. In two days I will stand on my feet and tend to the hooves of every beast in the village.
In our village pack mules and plow oxen wait unshod.
I forge crescent shoes, master! I make the cloven hooves of oxen hard as stone so the beast never stumbles while pulling the plow.
Yesterday we admitted the bugler whose tower was raided into the barracks; he warned that brigand horsemen were approaching.

The tower bugler? He spoke true, master! The three lead horses of those riders were about to split their hooves from lack of shoes; the troop trailing behind them will descend into this valley within two days. Let us shoe our horses so our cavalry stands ready!
We have few horses in our village, but many oxen and mules. Do you shoe them as well?

I trim the mule's hoof and nail crescent plates to the cloven hoof of the ox, gatekeeper! A beast whose hoof rots cannot haul a load. A farrier tends not to horses alone, but to the draft beasts of the entire village.
There is a strange brand on the horseshoes at your belt; whose horse was that?
It belonged to the caravan master's thoroughbred Arabian mount, master. The mark upon the shoe is the token of the Damascus caravan. It is not stolen, but a shoe of my own forging.
Will you aid the barracks cavalry with weapons and horseshoes?
I will enter the barracks stable! If a cavalry mount's hoof is not sound, the horse stumbles on the field of battle and throws its rider. I will inspect every mount.

yanitlar.kisla: Send me straight to the barracks stable! Let me inspect the hooves of the castle mounts and nail on the cast shoes. The cavalry's steeds will stay sound and never fail them mid-campaign.
yanitlar.kabul: I will crouch at the foot of the hay pile beside the stable, have Miraen Hatun bind my heel, and not stir till morning. Without burdening anyone, I will tend to my work.
yanitlar.ret: With this pierced foot I cannot take a step across the open steppe, gatekeeper... I will sit upon the threshold holding my pincers in my lap, yet if horsemen raid by night my blood will remain upon your gate.

not: Barracks, Accept, and Reject from the start.
acilis: I am an itinerant farrier of the caravan roads, gatekeeper... While shoeing a stallion at the waystation a raid broke out; the horse snapped its chain and trampled my heel, driving a horseshoe nail into my flesh. Hooking my pincers and this pair of shoes to my belt, I escaped through the moat culvert. If you have mounts, let them not go unshod—open the gate.
